set.detail: Flavius Honorius, born on 9 September 384 in Constantinople, was made Augustus at the age of eight in 393 and inherited the West at ten on his father Theodosius's death in January 395. His long reign of 28 years was dominated by others: first by Stilicho, who married him to his daughters Maria (398) and, after her death, Thermantia (408), then by the court officials Olympius and Jovius, and finally by the general Constantius, who married his half-sister Galla Placidia and became co-emperor in 421. Honorius moved the court from Milan to Ravenna in 402, protected by marshes, and rarely left it. His reign saw the invasion of Alaric (401-402) and Radagaisus (405-406), the crossing of the Rhine (406), the usurpation of Constantine III, the execution of Stilicho (408), the three sieges of Rome and the sack of 410, the loss of Britain, and the settlement of the Visigoths in Aquitaine (418). Procopius tells the story, probably apocryphal, that when told that Rome had perished he was upset, thinking of his favourite cockerel named Roma, and relieved to learn it was only the city. Yet his regime survived: the usurpers Constantine III, Jovinus, Maximus, Attalus and Heraclianus were all eliminated, and by 418 Constantius had restored a measure of stability in Gaul and Spain. Honorius's laws, numerous in the Theodosian Code, include measures against pagans, heretics and Donatists, and in 404 he banned gladiatorial combat after the death of the monk Telemachus in the arena, according to Theodoret. He quarrelled with Placidia, who fled to Constantinople in 423, and died of dropsy at Ravenna on 15 August 423, leaving no children.

scholarship: McEvoy, Child Emperor Rule in the Late Roman West (2013)
Doyle, Honorius: The Fight for the Roman West AD 395-423 (2019)

set.detail: Flavius Arcadius, elder son of Theodosius I and Aelia Flaccilla, was born in Spain around 377 and made Augustus in 383. He ruled the East from Constantinople from 395 until his death on 1 May 408 at the age of about 31. Contemporaries and later historians portrayed him as a weak, sleepy ruler dominated by his ministers and his wife: Synesius of Cyrene, in his speech On Kingship, implicitly criticises an emperor hidden in his palace. Power was exercised successively by the praetorian prefect Rufinus, murdered in 395; the eunuch grand chamberlain Eutropius, who arranged Arcadius's marriage in 395 to Aelia Eudoxia, daughter of the Frankish general Bauto, against Rufinus's plans, and who became consul in 399 before falling; the Gothic general Gainas, whose seizure of power in 400 ended in a massacre of Goths in the capital; Eudoxia, Augusta from 400, who clashed with John Chrysostom and had him exiled in 403-404; and finally the praetorian prefect Anthemius, from 405. Arcadius's reign saw recurrent conflict with the western court under Stilicho over Illyricum, the revolt of Alaric, the Hunnic raids through the Caucasus, the Isaurian raids, and the crisis of 399-400 over the role of Gothic soldiers. Yet the eastern empire was stabilised: the Goths were expelled from the capital, Alaric was directed westward, peace was kept with Persia, and Anthemius began the new land walls. Procopius reports that on his deathbed Arcadius appointed the Persian king Yazdegerd I as guardian of his son Theodosius II, a story that historians accept with caution. The column of Arcadius, erected in his forum, survives only as a base.

scholarship: Cameron and Long, Barbarians and Politics at the Court of Arcadius (1993)

set.detail: Theodosius II, born on 10 April 401, son of Arcadius and Eudoxia, was made Augustus at nine months in January 402 and became sole eastern emperor on his father's death in 408, at seven. His reign of 42 years was the longest of any Roman emperor. During his minority the praetorian prefect Anthemius governed effectively, building the land walls and stabilising the Danube. From 414 his elder sister Pulcheria, proclaimed Augusta, directed his education and the pious atmosphere of the court, where the imperial sisters took vows of virginity. In 421 he married Athenais, daughter of an Athenian sophist, baptised as Eudocia. Theodosius was studious, pious and a skilled calligrapher, nicknamed 'kalligraphos'. His government accomplished significant achievements: the founding of the higher school at the Capitol in 425, with chairs of Latin and Greek rhetoric and grammar, philosophy and law; the Theodosian Code (438); the restoration of the Theodosian dynasty in the West in 425; wars with Persia (421-422, 440-441) that preserved the frontier. Religious policy was dominated by the councils of Ephesus (431), which deposed Nestorius, and Ephesus II (449), which supported Eutyches. His relations with the Huns were costly: under Rua and then Attila and Bleda, the empire paid increasing tribute, culminating in 2,100 lb of gold a year after 447. In the 440s the eunuch Chrysaphius dominated the court, Eudocia retired to Jerusalem after a scandal involving the official Paulinus, and Pulcheria withdrew from court. Theodosius died on 28 July 450 after falling from his horse. Modern historians such as Millar have revised his reputation, stressing the effectiveness of his government.

scholarship: Harries, 'Pius princeps', in Harries and Wood (eds.), The Theodosian Code (1993)

set.detail: Aelia Galla Placidia, daughter of Theodosius I and his second wife Galla, was born around 390 and was in Rome when Alaric besieged it; she reportedly approved the Senate's execution of her cousin Serena in 408. Captured in the sack of 410, she remained with the Goths for five years and in January 414 married their king Athaulf at Narbonne, in a Roman ceremony at which Priscus Attalus sang the epithalamium and Athaulf presented her with fifty trays of gold and jewels from the sack of Rome. Their son Theodosius died in infancy at Barcelona. After Athaulf's murder in 415, Wallia returned her to the Romans in exchange for grain in 416, and on 1 January 417 Honorius forced her to marry the general Constantius, by whom she had Justa Grata Honoria and Valentinian. Constantius became Augustus in 421 and she Augusta, but he died months later; she quarrelled with Honorius, scandal followed, and in 423 she fled to Constantinople. With eastern help she installed her six-year-old son Valentinian III in 425 and governed the West as regent until about 437, the first woman to exercise power in the West in her own name for so long. Her regency was weakened by rivalry among the generals Felix, Bonifatius and Aetius, which contributed to the loss of Africa; after Bonifatius's death in 432 Aetius became dominant. She built churches in Ravenna, including San Giovanni Evangelista, vowed after surviving a storm at sea, and Santa Croce, to which the so-called Mausoleum of Galla Placidia is attached. She died in Rome on 27 November 450, during the Honoria affair. Her life embodies the interpenetration of the Roman and barbarian worlds.

scholarship: Sivan, Galla Placidia: The Last Roman Empress (2011)

set.detail: Flavius Placidus Valentinianus, born on 2 July 419 at Ravenna, son of Constantius III and Galla Placidia, was taken to Constantinople with his mother in 423 and installed in the West by an eastern army in 425, at six, after the fall of the usurper Joannes. He reigned for thirty years, the longest reign of any western emperor in the fifth century, though for most of it actual power lay first with his mother and then with Aetius. In 437 he married Licinia Eudoxia, daughter of Theodosius II, in Constantinople, ceding part of Illyricum to the East. His reign saw the loss of Africa to the Vandals (429-439), the treaty of 442 recognising their kingdom, the loss of much of Spain to the Suebi, the settlement of the Burgundians and Alans in Gaul, the invasions of Attila in Gaul (451) and Italy (452), and the Honoria affair. His laws, the Novels of Valentinian, illustrate the empire's fiscal crisis: they include the reduction of taxes for devastated provinces, the siliquaticum sales tax (444), measures on coloni and the recognition of papal authority in Gaul (445). Contemporaries portray him as frivolous, devoted to astrologers and pleasures, but his decision to assert himself by killing Aetius in September 454 with his own hands showed a will to rule. The murder cost him his life: on 16 March 455 two of Aetius's former guardsmen killed him on the Campus Martius, at the instigation of Petronius Maximus. With him the Theodosian dynasty ended in the West. He was buried in the mausoleum of the Theodosians at St Peter's in Rome. His daughters Eudocia and Placidia were taken to Carthage in 455.

scholarship: McEvoy, Child Emperor Rule in the Late Roman West (2013)
Heather, The Fall of the Roman Empire (2005)

set.detail: Aelia Pulcheria, born on 19 January 399, eldest daughter of Arcadius and Eudoxia, was proclaimed Augusta on 4 July 414, aged fifteen, and took charge of the education of her younger brother Theodosius II, displacing the prefect Anthemius. She and her sisters Arcadia and Marina took public vows of virginity, dedicated an altar in Hagia Sophia, and turned the palace into something like a convent, according to the church historian Sozomen, who dedicated his history to Theodosius and praises her. Her influence was largely religious: she promoted the cult of the Theotokos, collected relics, including those of St Stephen and the Forty Martyrs, built churches dedicated to the Virgin in Constantinople (the Chalkoprateia, Blachernae and Hodegetria were associated with her by later tradition), and supported Cyril of Alexandria against Nestorius, who had insulted her by refusing her access to the sanctuary and questioning her virginity. In the 440s her influence waned: the empress Eudocia and then the eunuch Chrysaphius dominated the court, and Pulcheria withdrew to the Hebdomon. On Theodosius's death in 450 she returned to power, chose the officer Marcian as emperor with the support of Aspar, and married him while remaining a virgin, conferring legitimacy on his rule as the last member of the Theodosian dynasty in the East. She had Chrysaphius executed and, with Marcian, summoned the Council of Chalcedon in 451, where she was acclaimed as a new Helena. She died in July 453 and left her property to the poor. The Orthodox church venerates her as a saint. Holum's study presents her as an example of the dynastic power of Theodosian women.

Marcian, born around 392 in Thrace or Illyricum, was a soldier of modest origins who served as domesticus (aide) to Ardabur and Aspar, fought in Persia in 421-422 and in Africa in 431, where, according to a legend in Procopius, he was captured by the Vandals and Gaiseric saw an eagle shading him as he slept, foretelling his rise. He was a retired tribune and senator when, after Theodosius II's death in July 450, Pulcheria and Aspar chose him as emperor; he married Pulcheria, who preserved her vow of virginity, and was proclaimed on 25 August 450. His seven-year reign was remembered as a golden age. He executed Chrysaphius, refused to pay tribute to Attila, and summoned the Council of Chalcedon (451), which condemned Eutyches and Dioscorus and defined the doctrine of two natures, with Marcian attending one session. Chalcedon caused revolts in Palestine and Egypt, which he suppressed. He sent troops to Italy in 452 that harassed Attila, and after Attila's death settled the Ostrogoths and other peoples of the former Hunnic empire as federates in Pannonia and Thrace. His fiscal policy was prudent: he remitted arrears of taxes, abolished the follis tax on senators, and reduced the burden of the praetorship. He left a full treasury, more than 100,000 lb of gold according to John Lydus. He did not intervene in the West after the Vandal sack of Rome in 455, perhaps under Aspar's influence. His column survives in Istanbul (Kıztaşı). He died on 27 January 457, probably of gangrene, and Aspar chose Leo, an officer of his household, as successor. The western court recognised Marcian only in 452.

Leo I, born around 401 in Dacia, was a military tribune in the household of Aspar, commanding a unit at Selymbria, when Aspar, unable to take the throne himself as an Arian of barbarian origin, chose him as emperor on Marcian's death in January 457. Leo was crowned on 7 February 457, according to tradition the first emperor crowned by the patriarch of Constantinople, Anatolius, a debated point. His seventeen-year reign was dominated by his effort to free himself from Aspar. To counterbalance the Gothic federates and their Germanic soldiers, he recruited Isaurians, promoting the Isaurian chieftain Tarasis, who took the name Zeno and married his daughter Ariadne in 466, and created a new palace guard, the excubitors. In 468, together with the western emperor Anthemius whom he had installed in 467, he launched a massive expedition against the Vandals under his brother-in-law Basiliscus, which ended in disaster at Cape Bon and cost the treasury 65,000 lb of gold. In 471 he had Aspar and his son Ardabur assassinated in the palace, earning the nickname Makelles, the butcher; the Gothic federates of Thrace under Theodoric Strabo rebelled, and Leo conceded their demands in 473. His reign also saw the end of the Huns under Dengizich (469), the Codex Encyclius on Chalcedon (457-458), the great fire of 465, and the arrival of the relic of the Virgin's robe at Blachernae. He supported Daniel the Stylite, who lived on a column near Constantinople. Leo died of dysentery on 18 January 474, leaving the throne to his grandson Leo II, son of Zeno and Ariadne, who crowned his father co-emperor and died the same year.

scholarship: Croke, 'Dynasty and ethnicity: Emperor Leo I and the eclipse of Aspar', Chiron 35 (2005)

set.detail: Zeno, born around 425 with the name Tarasis (Tarasicodissa), son of Kodisa, from Rousoumblada in Isauria, was a chieftain recruited by Leo I as a counterweight to Aspar. In 466 he exposed Ardabur's treasonous correspondence with Persia, married Leo's daughter Ariadne, and took the Greek name Zeno. He was magister militum per Orientem and consul (469). When his young son Leo II succeeded Leo I in January 474, he had Zeno crowned co-emperor on 9 February; the boy died in November. Zeno's reign of 17 years was marked by instability. In January 475 a conspiracy of the empress Verina, her brother Basiliscus and the Isaurian Illus drove him from the capital; he returned in August 476, after Basiliscus had alienated the city with his anti-Chalcedonian encyclical. Zeno then faced a revolt of Marcian (479), the competing Gothic leaders Theodoric Strabo and Theodoric the Amal in the Balkans, and the revolt of Illus and Leontius (484-488). He resolved the Gothic problem by sending Theodoric the Amal to Italy against Odoacer in 488, after Strabo's death. In the West, he received the imperial insignia from Odoacer in 476 and recognised Julius Nepos until 480. In religion, he issued the Henotikon (482), drafted by the patriarch Acacius, a formula of union that avoided the question of Chalcedon; it reconciled Egypt but caused the Acacian Schism with Rome (484-519). He closed the school of Edessa in 489 and suppressed the Samaritan revolt of 484. He died on 9 April 491, perhaps of epilepsy or dysentery. Later Isaurian unpopularity and hostile sources such as Malchus coloured his reputation.

scholarship: Elton, 'Illus and the imperial aristocracy under Zeno', Byzantion 70 (2000)

set.detail: Anastasius, born around 431 at Dyrrachium, was a silentiarius, an usher of the palace, of about sixty, known for his piety and his miaphysite sympathies, when the empress Ariadne chose him as Zeno's successor in April 491 and married him. The patriarch Euphemius made him sign a written profession of Chalcedonian orthodoxy before his coronation. His reign of 27 years was one of the most successful in Roman history in administrative and financial terms. He removed the Isaurians from power, defeating them in the Isaurian War (492-497). He reformed the copper coinage in 498 with large folles marked with their value (M = 40 nummi), stabilising petty money; abolished the chrysargyron, the hated tax on traders, in 498, burning the records publicly; and gave responsibility for collecting municipal taxes to imperial officials (vindices), with the help of the Syrian praetorian prefect Marinus. He left 320,000 lb of gold in the treasury according to Procopius. He fought a war against Persia (502-506), in which Amida fell, and built the fortress of Dara (505) and the Long Walls of Thrace. In the Balkans he faced Bulgar raids. His religious policy, favouring the miaphysites and the Henotikon, led him to depose the Chalcedonian patriarchs Euphemius (496) and Macedonius II (511), and to appoint Severus at Antioch (512). This provoked the Trisagion riots of 512, in which Anastasius appeared without his diadem in the Hippodrome and offered to abdicate, and the revolt of Vitalian (513-515). He died on 9 July 518, aged about 88. The sources nicknamed him Dicorus because his eyes had different colours.

Justin, born around 450 in Bederiana near Naissus in Dardania into a Latin-speaking peasant family, went to Constantinople as a young man with two companions, according to Procopius on foot with only bread in their bags, and joined the palace guard of the excubitors created by Leo I. He served in the Isaurian War under Anastasius, in the Persian war (502-506), and against Vitalian in 515, by then commander of the excubitors. When Anastasius died without an heir in July 518, Justin, by then nearly seventy, was chosen in a disputed process, allegedly using money given to him by the eunuch Amantius to promote another candidate. His reign of nine years marked the return to Chalcedonian orthodoxy: in 519 he ended the Acacian Schism with Rome by accepting the formula of Pope Hormisdas, removed Severus of Antioch and other miaphysite bishops, and persecuted the miaphysites in Syria. In the East, he received the Lazic king Tzath, who converted to Christianity in Constantinople (522), took Iberia's King Gourgenes under protection, and rejected Kavad's request to adopt his son Khosrow (525), which led to war in 526-527. In the West, his pressure on Arians led to the crisis with Theodoric in 525-526. His nephew Justinian, whom he had adopted and educated, was the real power; Justin made him Caesar and finally co-emperor on 1 April 527. Procopius in the Secret History mocks Justin as illiterate, using a stencil to sign his name, and as dominated by Justinian. He died on 1 August 527 of an infected ulcer on his foot. His wife Lupicina-Euphemia, a former slave, opposed Justinian's marriage to Theodora.

Justinian, born Petrus Sabbatius around 482 at Tauresium in Dardania into a Latin-speaking family, was brought to Constantinople by his uncle Justin, who had him educated and adopted him. Under Justin (518-527) he was the dominant figure, consul in 521, Caesar and then co-emperor in April 527, sole emperor from August 527 until his death in November 565. Around 525 he married Theodora, after Justin changed the law forbidding senators to marry former actresses. His reign was the most ambitious since Constantine. In law, his commission under Tribonian produced the Code (529, 534), the Digest and Institutes (533), and he issued over 150 Novels, many in Greek. In war, after a Persian war ended by the Eternal Peace (532), he reconquered Africa (533-534), Italy (535-554), Sicily, Sardinia and Corsica, and part of southern Spain (552); but the renewed Persian war (540-562), with the sack of Antioch and the struggle for Lazica, and the raids of Bulgars, Slavs and Kutrigurs strained resources. He nearly lost his throne in the Nika riot (532), after which he rebuilt Hagia Sophia (532-537) and many other buildings described by Procopius in the Buildings. In religion, he sought to impose orthodoxy on pagans (closure of the Athenian school, 529), Samaritans, Jews and heretics, while trying to reconcile miaphysites through the condemnation of the Three Chapters (544, 553), which alienated the West. The plague of 541-542 struck the empire and the emperor himself. Procopius praised him in the Buildings and denounced him as a demon in the Secret History. Modern assessments range from a great restorer to a ruler who overreached, leaving his successors an overextended and impoverished empire.

scholarship: Maas (ed.), The Cambridge Companion to the Age of Justinian (2005)

set.detail: Theodora, born around 500, perhaps in Paphlagonia or Cyprus, was the daughter of Acacius, a bear-keeper of the Greens in the Hippodrome of Constantinople, and an actress. After her father's death, according to Procopius, the Greens refused to help her mother, but the Blues took the family in, which explains her later support of the Blues. She became an actress and courtesan, and the Secret History describes her performances in lurid detail. She became the mistress of Hecebolus, governor of Libya Pentapolis, was abandoned, and on her way back through Alexandria and Antioch came into contact with miaphysite leaders, notably Timothy III and Severus of Antioch. In Constantinople she met Justinian, who married her around 525 after his uncle changed the law forbidding senators to marry actresses. She was crowned Augusta on 1 April 527. Theodora had considerable influence. Procopius credits her with a speech during the Nika riot (532) urging Justinian not to flee, with the line 'royalty is a good burial shroud'. She protected the miaphysites, sheltering hundreds of monks and bishops in the palace of Hormisdas and supporting the missions of Jacob Baradaeus and the Nubian mission of Julian; she promoted the deposition of Pope Silverius and the election of Vigilius. She was credited with laws protecting women, against forced prostitution and on dowries, and with a convent for former prostitutes, the Metanoia. She led the intrigue against John the Cappadocian in 541. She died of cancer, perhaps, on 28 June 548. Her portrait in the mosaics of San Vitale in Ravenna is one of the most famous images of late antiquity. Modern historians consider Procopius's account largely as invective.

scholarship: Cameron, Procopius and the Sixth Century (1985)

set.detail: Justin II, born around 520, son of Justinian's sister Vigilantia and Dulcidius, married Sophia, niece of Theodora. As curopalates (head of palace administration) in the last years of Justinian's reign, he was in the palace when the old emperor died on 14-15 November 565, and with the support of the Senate and of Tiberius, commander of the excubitors, he was crowned at once, before his rival cousin Justin, son of Germanus, could act. Corippus's panegyric In laudem Iustini describes the coronation ceremony in detail. He began by paying Justinian's debts and remitting arrears of taxes, but adopted a haughty foreign policy: he refused the subsidies to the Avars (565), causing them to move toward the Lombards and Gepids, and in 572 refused the payment due to Persia under the treaty of 562, supporting the Armenian revolt and allying with the Western Turks. The results were disastrous: the Lombards invaded Italy in 568, the Avars took Pannonia and threatened Sirmium, the Visigoths attacked Spania, and the Persians took Dara in 573. Justin's religious policy, after attempts at compromise with the miaphysites, turned to persecution from 571. Justin had his rival cousin killed in 566. The loss of Dara drove him mad: John of Ephesus describes his fits of biting, being pulled around in a cart, and organ music played to calm him. Sophia took over the government and bought a truce from Persia; in December 574 Justin adopted Tiberius and made him Caesar, in a speech recorded by Theophylact advising him not to follow his example. He died on 5 October 578 after Tiberius had been made Augustus. The couple appear on coins seated together.

scholarship: Cameron, 'The early religious policies of Justin II', Studies in Church History 13 (1976)
Whitby, The Emperor Maurice and His Historian (1988)

set.detail: Tiberius, born around 535 in Thrace, was a notary and protégé of the patriarch Eutychius, then commander of the excubitors under Justin II. He helped Justin take the throne in 565 and fought the Avars around 570, being defeated. When Justin went mad in 574, Sophia and Justin chose him as Caesar on 7 December 574, with the name Tiberius Constantinus; he became Augustus on 26 September 578 and sole emperor on Justin's death on 5 October 578. Sophia, who had hoped to marry him, was angered when he brought his wife Ino, renamed Anastasia, to the palace, and conspired with the general Justinian to replace him. Tiberius was famous for his generosity: he distributed vast sums to the people and the army, reduced taxes by a quarter, and abolished the tax on wine supplies, exhausting the treasury accumulated by Justin II. He continued the Persian war, his generals Justinian and Maurice winning at Melitene (576) and in Arzanene (578), while negotiations failed on the death of Khosrow I (579). He used subsidies to manage the Avars and Lombards, but lost Sirmium to the Avars in 582 and could not prevent Slav settlement in the Balkans. In Italy, he bribed Lombard dukes and sent money to the Franks to attack them. He recruited a new army of 15,000 foreign soldiers, the Foederati, under Maurice's command. Gregory of Tours, who praises him, tells that he found a hidden treasure under the floor of the palace marked with a cross. He fell ill in August 582, apparently from bad mulberries, and died on 14 August 582, having designated Maurice as successor, married to his daughter Constantina.

scholarship: Whitby, The Emperor Maurice and His Historian (1988)

set.detail: Flavius Mauricius Tiberius, born in 539 at Arabissus in Cappadocia, was a notary who became comes excubitorum under Tiberius II and magister militum per Orientem in 578. He raided Arzanene and Persia (578-581), took part in the abortive expedition with the Ghassanid al-Mundhir (581), defeated the Persians at Constantina (582), and was chosen by the dying Tiberius as successor, crowned on 13 August 582, and married to his daughter Constantina. His reign of twenty years was one of hard struggle against limited resources. In the East, the Persian war continued until the civil war that brought Bahram Chobin to power gave him the opportunity to restore Khosrow II (591), receiving Dara, Martyropolis and much of Armenia; the peace freed his army for the Balkans, where his generals Priscus, Peter and Comentiolus fought the Avars and Slavs from 592 to 602, taking the war north of the Danube. In the West, he created the exarchates of Ravenna and Carthage, combining civil and military authority, financed the Franks against the Lombards, and in 597 drafted a will dividing the empire among his sons. The Strategikon, a military manual, is traditionally attributed to him. His economy measures, made necessary by an empty treasury, made him unpopular: a reduction in military pay caused a mutiny in 588, his refusal to ransom 12,000 prisoners from the Avars in 599 led to their massacre, and the order to winter beyond the Danube in 602 caused the revolt of Phocas. He was executed with his sons at Chalcedon on 27 November 602. Theophylact's history, written under Heraclius, is the main source, presenting him as a pious martyr.

scholarship: Whitby, The Emperor Maurice and His Historian (1988)

set.detail: Phocas, born around 547 in Thrace, was a centurion of the Danube army who had been sent on a deputation of soldiers to Constantinople in 601 and humiliated by the patrician Comentiolus. In November 602, when the army mutinied against Maurice's order to winter beyond the Danube, the soldiers raised him on a shield. He marched on Constantinople, where the Greens supported him; Maurice fled and Phocas was crowned at the Hebdomon on 23 November 602. He had Maurice and his sons executed on 27 November. His reign of eight years was later described, by sources written under his successor Heraclius, as a tyranny: he executed Maurice's supporters and many aristocrats, including Maurice's widow Constantina and her daughters, the general Narses, who had rebelled in Edessa, and the patrician Germanus. His statues and the Column of Phocas in the Roman Forum, dedicated by the exarch Smaragdus on 1 August 608, show that he enjoyed good relations with the papacy: Pope Gregory welcomed his accession, and Phocas recognised the primacy of the Roman see and allowed Pope Boniface IV to convert the Pantheon into a church (609). Militarily his reign was a disaster: Khosrow II declared war to avenge Maurice, conquering Mesopotamia and Armenia, while Avars and Slavs advanced in the Balkans. Riots between Blues and Greens broke out in many cities. In 608 the exarch of Africa, Heraclius the Elder, rebelled; his nephew Nicetas took Egypt and his son Heraclius sailed for Constantinople, where the Greens and the excubitors abandoned Phocas. He was executed on 5 October 610. Modern historians, notably Olster, warn that his image derives from the propaganda of the Heraclian dynasty.

scholarship: Olster, The Politics of Usurpation in the Seventh Century (1993)

set.detail: Heraclius, born around 575 in Cappadocia, son of Heraclius the Elder, a general of Armenian origin and from 600 exarch of Africa, led the fleet that overthrew Phocas and was crowned emperor on 5 October 610. He inherited a disastrous situation: the Persians conquered Syria (613), Jerusalem (614), where they took the True Cross, and Egypt (619), and reached Chalcedon (615), while the Avars and Slavs overran the Balkans. After years of reorganisation, financing the war with church treasures and halving salaries, in 622 he took the field in person, beginning a series of campaigns deep in Persian territory: Atropatene (624), where he destroyed the fire temple of Adur Gushnasp, the Caucasus (625-626), the alliance with the Western Turks and the siege of Tiflis (627), and the decisive victory at Nineveh (627). Meanwhile, Constantinople survived the Avar-Persian siege of 626. The fall of Khosrow II (628) brought peace and the return of all Roman territory and the True Cross, which Heraclius restored to Jerusalem in 630. But the Arab invasions began within a few years: Syria was lost after the Yarmuk (636), followed by Jerusalem, Mesopotamia and Egypt. His attempt to reconcile Chalcedonians and miaphysites through monoenergism (633) and the Ekthesis (638) failed. His second marriage to his niece Martina was considered incestuous. His reign saw the use of the title basileus (629) and the decline of Latin in government. He died on 11 February 641. His reign is one of the most dramatic in Roman history, between triumph and catastrophe, and he became a figure of medieval legend associated with the Exaltation of the Cross.

scholarship: Reinink and Stolte (eds.), The Reign of Heraclius (2002)
Howard-Johnston, Witnesses to a World Crisis (2010)

set.detail: Flavius Stilicho, born around 359, son of a Vandal cavalry officer and a Roman mother, rose under Theodosius I, who sent him as envoy to Persia around 383 and married him to his niece and adopted daughter Serena. He commanded at the Frigidus (394) and on Theodosius's death in 395 claimed to be guardian of both sons, effectively ruling the West for Honorius, whom he married to his daughters Maria and later Thermantia. His thirteen years in power were spent in constant crisis: he fought Alaric in Greece (395, 397), crushed the revolt of Gildo in Africa (398), defeated Alaric at Pollentia and Verona (402) and destroyed Radagaisus at Faesulae (406). He was in permanent conflict with the eastern court over Illyricum, being declared a public enemy in Constantinople (397), and sought to use Alaric to seize eastern Illyricum (407). His critics accused him of letting the barbarians in, of withdrawing troops from the Rhine and Britain, and of favouring barbarians; Rutilius claims he burned the Sibylline books and Orosius accuses him of plotting to put his son Eucherius on the throne. When the Rhine was breached (406), Constantine III took Gaul, and Alaric demanded 4,000 lb of gold, which Stilicho forced the Senate to pay, his position weakened. A court conspiracy led by Olympius provoked a mutiny at Ticinum in August 408, and Stilicho, refusing to let his barbarian troops fight the Roman soldiers, was executed at Ravenna on 22 August 408. His death led to the massacre of barbarian soldiers' families and their desertion to Alaric. Claudian's poems are his main propaganda.
